utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I mention two housekeeping matters before we begin. Firstly, on Thursday morning, the Trial Chamber will be hearing another matter at 9.00 a.m. We expect to finish that matter by the end of the first break, so the parties should be on stand-by to recommence this trial at 10.30, that's the beginning of the second session. Secondly, I understand that we will not have any German interpretation for tomorrow, but my expectation is that we will conclude this witness's testimony today with the cooperation of Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hartwig, we left off talking about your experiences in Pristina. What was the relationship or attitude of the ordinary Albanians towards the political situation?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: One has to differentiate between those who helped to form public opinion and those for whom it was just a matter of their own lives and survival. The average Albanian was actually less interested in politics, but he was interested in establishing foundations for his economic survival irrespective of external influences for managing his life. That was the average Albanian. Of course, there was certainly also, among these one or the other, who was pleased to make promises or follow promises from Albanian politicians for -- who promised a better life under different conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, were any rights curtailed with regard to the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally heard only general complaints that most of the Serbs have. They have done one or the other thing. But in personal discussions, I never heard any reprimands against any particular person or individual offices of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, did you ever have an opportunity of asking anybody? Did you ever ask anyone whether they were lacking in some rights and -- or anything else; and if so, what? Denied any rights?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two cases, and I made inquiries specifically about these. First of all, there was the complaints that the people at the university did not use their language, and I then spoke to the head of the university, and he said that in the first semester for the curriculum and the general administrative rules the Serbian language would be used, but otherwise there was also the possibility, depending on the ethnic relationship of the participants, that they could speak Albanian. The second case, we lived in the house belonging to a doctor couple, and we heard that the man lost his position in the ministry because of his -- because he was Albanian, and the same applied to his wife and applied also to the son and to the daughter. But I heard in a talk that the father didn't lose his position because of his Albanian nationality but because he had simply reached retirement age. And in this period, the mother gave up her professorship at the university to be together with her husband, and the son was in hospital because -- had problems in the hospital because did he not want to operate on a Serb, and the daughter was training to be a specialist doctor. This statement I heard from an Albanian, and that is from the daughter, and this seemed to me to be credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me something about the attitude of the Albanian population or individual groups or categories of the Albanian population towards your own mission. Or let me be more specific: Were there any cases where your cars would be stopped, the vehicles belonging to your mission would be stopped by members of the KLA, intercepted?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only ones that ever stopped us or ever stopped me in Kosovo were members of the KLA, or they had set up roadblocks in territories governed by the KLA, and therefore, they did not have a diplomatic pass, just the personal appearance and -- but they were -- did not respect diplomatic passes. But as I said, we were stopped, and in individual cases people did shoot at our vehicles, but we had armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you said people shot, who shot at your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure who shot, but certainly either it was in the zone controlled by the KLA, but also -- although that was not the case in my case, but somewhere near Stimlje where this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And would you say that the KLA was a terrorist organisation, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only compare with an organisation that one heard about quite a lot in my country, that is the Red Army Faction, and these people wanted to have another republic, and they were designated terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how would you qualify the goals and the means of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a grouping is concerned with means, using peaceful means, then one can establish a democracy. But the means that were adopted there did not comply with democratic means. They were, in my opinion, very clearly beyond legality, and also the actions that were started with these means were beyond legality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you have already told us, you met many members of the KLA. How would you qualify the leaders of the KLA? What would you say about them?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't meet the higher people in the KLA but just those that you could call middle management. In principle, these were very simple commanders who quite simply wanted the Albanians to have the sole decision rights in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the attitude of the KLA leaders towards the Serbs, for instance, and other non-Albanians, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a personal statement, I think I already mentioned that. In the unofficial version of the constitution of Kosovo, there was a paragraph that they should not continue to live under or with the Serbs, but nothing had been said about the other ethnic groups. And later I read about this in the newspaper, and therefore this is secondhand information for which I would not like to give my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is your impression, or what knowledge do you have throughout the time you spent in Kosovo and Metohija about who caused the problems during that period of time that you were there? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the origin of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. It's too general, and it just invites mere opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, according to your knowledge and information and judging by what you were able to see and learn, led to problems, caused problems in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the same thing. Move on to another question, Mr. Milosevic. Let's bring this to an end now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, were there any attacks launched by the KLA on police stations?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't just attacks against police stations, also attacks at individual police out on patrol. And I believe that ultimately that was the policy, to make such attacks against the executive power of that country, because as a rule they used -- they used to expect to have searches being made. They also probably expected actions which could be seen as very negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain that to us a little better, please?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there was an attack against a civilian, then without doubt it is possible that in a country where perhaps it's normal for a man to carry a weapon, that this escalates into a shoot-out between individuals. At the moment where the executive branch would come into play, that is then not normally a man-to-man fight but it becomes a collective action instead perpetrated by a unit of the police or security forces directed against not one man or individual but directed, rather, against a group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I must say I'm not following you well enough. It's not clear enough. Did the forces of law and order react to the KLA, to the KLA attacks?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, most of the actions undertaken by the security forces were reactions to incidents, happenings which had been perpetrated by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the KLA hide behind civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. That's -- you can't ask that. That's clearly leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, did you happen to talk to the leaders of the police, our police, for instance, in Kosovo with respect to the risks that civilians were running during these provocations on the part of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly talked to people. As I mentioned, with General Djukic, for example, but I also, and I can't remember -- there was the police chief of Malisevo with whom I've had an extensive discussion on which were the risks which resulted from ambush situations, from attacks against members of the executive and also members of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you asked Mr. Hartwig, Did the forces of law and order react to the KLA, to the KLA attacks, and he said that as far as he knew, most of the actions undertaken by the forces were reactions to incidents, happenings which had been perpetrated by the other side. It would obviously strengthen your case if you could direct Mr. Hartwig or ask him if he was able to identify any specific incidents where the official forces, security forces, reacted to incidents, because that might go towards a defence of self-defence. But as it is, it has just been left at a very general -- very general level. But you're facing an indictment with many allegations of violence by security forces, and it would clearly help your case if you could bring evidence to show that this violence, the alleged crimes were committed as a reaction and in a proportionate way to action taken by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, you have heard what Mr. Robinson has just said, and he explained it very well. Could you please now confirm or refute that the conduct of the security forces in Kosovo was a reaction to the attacks from the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're facing an indictment with specific allegations of incidents happening at a particular village, in a particular municipality where so many people were beaten or killed. Just to have him give -- to make general conclusory remarks is not what we're really looking for. In preparing the witness, you should have sought to find out whether he was in a position to give that kind of evidence. I mean, he was there. In his work with the ECMM, he might have received reports which would have confirmed that the security forces were acting responsibly to the attacks by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, can you quote some examples of such events having taken place where the forces of law and order reacted to attacks from the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: These events are almost six years back. I know I have notes in which KLA attacks are described and where, as a result, some of the attackers were injured or even killed, but currently I'm afraid I can't give you an exact statement telling you this happened in this place or that place or it was this or that incident exactly. But it were -- these were incidents which effected attacks against the police as well as also sometimes military personnel. Perhaps one example, if I am allowed to mention this: Kotlina, Ivaja, and Gajre, there the radio had said this was an arbitrary action undertaken on the part of the security forces. However, in the course of the discussion, I heard that it was from, I think, Pudina [phoen], but I'm not entirely sure about the exact name, but people shot from somewhere in the hills on bridges below, so that basically that action directed against the three villages can be seen as a reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, I do realise that a lot of time has gone by since then, but if we look at the chronology of events from the time you were the head of the -- of the monitoring mission in Kosovo, I'm going to quote and go through a few events and ask you whether you remember them or not. For example, let's start with January 1999, for instance, and I'll skip over the previous points. On the 5th of January, a MUP patrol came upon an ambush at Suva Reka. Four policemen were seriously wounded. Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was one of the first large-scale ambushes. And if I'm not wrong, this was near Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hartwig. Now, do you remember the 8th of January? Let's once again skip over a few days and go to the 8th of January when three officers of the MUP were killed from an ambush and three civilians wounded when eight soldiers -- and this all took place on the 8th of January -- was kidnapped by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the accused is reading from a document that's available to the Chamber, no doubt the Chamber would like to know what the document is. If he is reading from one of the proposed exhibits of the witness, he should identify which tab. My observation is that thus far, the accused is giving more detail than is contained in the only tab in the witness's exhibit file that relates to these matters. So I don't know what he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what are you reading from, if anything? Are you quoting from a document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am reading from my own chronological notes reflecting events from the time when Mr. Hartwig headed the monitoring mission. I presume that he remembers the 8th of January when three policemen and eight soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia were killed and kidnapped respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is simply leading. If he turns to I think it is tab 2 of the witness's materials, he will find an abbreviated reference to these topics, and an appropriate way, if he wants to go into it, would be to say, and I'm looking at the document headed 14th of June, I think, of 1999, but then typed headed the 6th to the 13th of January, 1999 -- tab 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I left my tabbed version upstairs. I'm grateful to Your Honour. Tab 3, of course,. And if you look at the foot of the first paragraph, you will see references to either 3 MUP in a KLA ambush. We can certainly track the date of that to the 8th of January. If the accused wants detail of that from this witness, then one way he could deal with that without leading the detail himself from whatever records he's relying on is to ask the witness to amplify the entry on the document. Whether that's what he wants to do, I don't know. But simply him reading out his version of the documents won't be satisfactory to the Chamber, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. I shall adhere to the exhibits, and they are perfectly sufficient to explain the situation. Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice has just mentioned tab 3. I will not even linger on the bottom of the page that he described. Just tell us before we start with this, Mr. Hartwig, what does WSS mean -- WASS? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an abbreviation for weekly assessment. This is a type of report which I had to submit on a weekly basis to mission headquarters. And this was based on the daily reports submitted by individual teams and also used information from additional talks I had and information and intelligence we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Hartwig, this weekly overview of events, as you said, is dated 21st of January, 1999. It's tab 3. I shall draw your attention to page 2, because it gives a dense account of a multitude of events, and it mentions EU-KDOM relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if the date is 21st, then it should be tab 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. In my binder it's tab 3. I must have made a mistake in arranging the tabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, yes, it says here, Weekly Assessment, 6 to 13th January, tab 3. Paragraph one says: "... explosion of a hand grenade in front of a cafe at Pristina, the murder of the Serb manager of the Obilic power plant, the killing of 3 MUP in a KLA ambush, and the capturing of 8 VJ soldiers by KLA." So this is covered in your weekly report. Does it refresh your memory as to these events, because they are contained in your daily and weekly reports?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the moment I can remember the word the manager of the power station Obilic, the story with the murder and under which circumstances they were -- they were killed in an ambush. I'm afraid the details of this I'm not familiar with, but as far as I recall, they used part of a street which formed some of the control area of KLA, and that the capture -- that the capture on the side of the international community caused some disquiet, the capturing of the VJ soldiers. But I cannot recall details as to how and under which circumstances now patrols of the security forces were attacked or how individual policemen were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I suppose this explosion of a hand grenade in front of a cafe in Pristina and the killing of the manager of the power plant in Obilic and the killing of three policemen, as it says here, from an ambush and the kidnapping of soldiers were events that were doubtlessly recorded and verified by your monitors. That's what it says in this weekly assessment.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there is nothing in this report that was just imaginary. The hand grenade attack in Pristina, which as far as I can recall, actually, was the first attack within a city, within a town, and I said at that time that the war had been transferred to the town after I think also something similar had happened in Pec before that. But this was significant as an event because that village was the main town of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hartwig.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pristina, I'm sorry, was the main town of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Hartwig. Let us just go through a number of these tabs. Please look at tab 5, dated 28th of January, 1999. In paragraph 2 under paragraph 1, it says: "After KLA attacks against police cars [In English] with eight policemen injured, MUP surrounded a house at Mitrovica covering approximately 12 KLA fighters; MUP ordered to surrender twice - but the response was small-arms fire. When KLA tried to escape, two fighters were killed and the others escaped." [Interpretation] That's the event. And now comes this sentence which is very typical, so I would appreciate your comment on this. "[In English] In public, the two KLA fighters were described as victims of MUP violence and caused clear demonstrations of Albania solidarity." [Interpretation] Mr. Hartwig, you are a German officer with a great amount of experience, and you know this event that is described here. So vehicles -- not one vehicle but vehicles of the police were attacked, eight policemen were wounded. The police surrounds a house, only the house where the perpetrators are located. The police invite them twice to surrender, with the intention to arrest them, as any police would do. However, the perpetrators respond with fire, tried to break out, and in the attempt, two of them get killed. This is then portrayed as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just ask the question without making comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- as a sacrifice on the part of the attackers. Well, Mr. Hartwig, I will ask him [as interpreted] some more questions based on the events, but from this event and the previous events, was the conduct of our law enforcement and security forces an aggressive one or was it, rather, contained? In other words, would you characterise it as normal behaviour on the part of law enforcement and security forces, by your standards?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not have the document here, so I'll just follow what has been said, that in this incident both OSCE was there, but also members of our own mission were there, and it was not mentioned in our report that the security forces were aggressive in any manner or -- or that they behaved in an excessive manner. It was a normal police action, which actually must be regarded as having been normal. The claimed perpetrators flee into a house, they barricade themselves, the house is surrounded, and the people in there are then called upon to put down their arms and to surrender. So this was a topic of our evaluation afterwards. And it should be said that the -- or to say that the police did not behave correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think the witness should have his binder in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, I'm sorry, I thought all the time that you had the documents in front of you. I thought they had been put in front of you, and that's why I quoted and invoked certain paragraphs. This is paragraph 5 that we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 5.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Tab 5, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I read out to you part of paragraph 2 from page 1, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in the middle of paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he has already commented on that, Mr. Milosevic, without the tab in front of him, so you can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, what I'm asking you now refers not only to this incident but to your entire experience as head of the monitors in Kosovo and Metohija. Would you say that law enforcement and security forces behaved aggressively or showed restraint?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had no statements as to the police having been behaved aggressively in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. But let me ask you a more precise question now. To the best of your knowledge from all the time that you spent there, did security forces ever attack the KLA first?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I refer to what was given to me as part of my task and what I heard from my team and what I myself saw and experienced or received in reports, but according to that, as a rule we're concerned here with reactions on the part of the security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Hartwig.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I would like the witness to deal with the paragraph which is at the foot of the same page. What was the basis of this observation, and what was the reason for him to put this paragraph in his report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I read the paragraph, Mr. Kwon? You mean the one that begins with: "This is the classic and normal development..."?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] "... classic and normal development: Attempts and assassinations by KLA against police MUP -- against police/MUP which - in turn - allegedly try to identify and arrest the perpetrators ... but where and how police/MUP search for and identify them? After the operations, weapons are hidden and the fighters convert to normal citizens with no visible link to KLA. Since it is not the speciality of Serb forces and impossible under those conditions to surgically conduct operations, the hammering seems to remain the only response. It can be expected that, as long as KLA applies its guerrilla tactics, the proceeding of police/MUP and VJ against KLA will remain unchanged."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, Mr. Kwon wanted you to comment on this paragraph as well, the one from your report.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this paragraph, I stated one of the fundamentals of partisan fighting. This does not relate specifically to KLA or security forces of the Serbs, but this is a generally applicable recipe which one finds in all wars, used in partisan battles. But one mixes among the civil population in the hopes that the moral barriers of those attacks are so high that nothing will happen. But this is simply wishful thinking in most wars in the past, and certainly this type of partisan fighting is very specific, and in principle it has rules that certainly have been laid down in terms of common law, but in practice they are very difficult to adhere to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is your general observation at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To just add to that, it is does not relate specifically to this situation; it is a general observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, from your contacts with chiefs of police, did you hear anything about their efforts to avoid civilian casualties at all costs?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood this correctly, acoustically, so perhaps you could repeat that. Would you be so kind as to repeat the question, please. I simply didn't hear it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. In your contacts with chiefs of police, police administration, were you informed of all the steps taken by the police to avoid civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard anything about this. Probably in the situation, I wouldn't have asked that specific question because tactics of -- in this kind of conflict are such that it is virtually impossible to really direct what is happening unless you completely ignore such attacks and simply accept them without comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, if, in response to their attacks, our forces used disproportionate force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, in my view, he shouldn't be asked the question in that way. Ask him specifically what kind of force was used, and then we will assess the proportionality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I am bearing in mind that Mr. Hartwig said at the very outset that he had served for 30 years in the German army, that he had dealt extensively with these affairs and issues. He headed a monitoring mission. I presume that he had to come face-to-face with the fact that disproportionate force was being used if it was indeed used. He had several months of practice, direct involvement in Kosovo. I'm simply asking if, in his opinion, disproportionate force was used there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, you were there. What kind of force was used by the armed forces in response to the KLA attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, after an attack they started looking for the perpetrators, and when approaching a possible scene, there were still shots being fired from some of the villages. And as part of a simple search of houses, people were arrested, and certainly people were also taken away for questioning. There may -- yes, there were cases, actually, that when there was stronger shooting from these villages, that then the police forces would have used heavy machine-guns in reply. During the time I was there, at any rate, no heavy arms were used, at least not until, let's say, the last ten days or so before evacuation. That was a time when I heard from Podpuzuve [phoen], that area in the north, that there was artillery fire occasionally. But until that time, they didn't use heavy arms; light artillery weapons were employed. And KLA attacks were also done with artillery weapons with anti-tank grenades and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I will allow you to comment on the proportionality, because I now recollect that several Prosecution witnesses did comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only reply something which I was told in a discussion with -- someone said if people could do as they would like to do, he said then we, the Serbs, would probably have managed to cope with the KLA. And I think the way he used the word "cope" was not in a general sense of eliminating the threat but perhaps might have meant they would have used sufficient pressure on the KLA that they might have been forced to negotiate as a result. But there was the statement that if they had been given a free hand, they would have had more opportunities. That was a statement made in my hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you heard that, did you have the impression or maybe was it said explicitly that their activities were minimised, reduced to pure self-defence?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not mentioned that activities were reduced, but it was stated unequivocally that these were not security forces' actions which were executed in an arbitrary matter. It was also made very clear that it was the job of the security forces to ensure that all people living in Kosovo, irrespective of their ethnicity, could be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While we are still at tab 5, let me draw your attention to item 2, which in this report as well seems to confirm your notes that we saw in tab 1. In item 2, in your own text, the report of the 28th of January, it says: "The Rector of the Albanian University of Pristina stated [In English] 'Not under the Serbs and not with the Serbs,' the new Albanian constitution does not acknowledge Serbs as a national minority and Albanians engaged in watching human rights cannot imagine at all to think of some type of co-existence with Serbs." [Interpretation] And then he says: "[In English] This, together with the strong ongoing Albanian demand NATO to militarily interfere indicate that no political resolutions with the Serbs are sought or even preferred any more. "The Albanian side only needs to continue with its tactics of stitches, just waiting for the (anticipated) Serb reactions - and sooner or later, the international community will react in one or the other way." [Interpretation] Mr. Hartwig, we're not talking about the rights of Albanians here. What this refers to is, as you yourself said and mentioned, you were told by rector of the Albanian University, that they wished that -- to see no more Serbs in Kosovo. So was that the clear message sent out to them? Is that how you understood it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if he wants to make things difficult for the witness, but he seems to have overlooked the second paragraph that leads "President Rugova's spokesman..." He didn't read that out. Maybe the witness ought to have the whole passage in mind before he's asked to give the sort of answer that's sought by the latest general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a matter you could raise in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can do, but from the witness's point of view, it's unfortunate if something is taken completely out of context. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, what the spokesman said, Rugova's spokesman said does not carry the same weight as what the witness was told by the rector of the university, because the rector of the university tells him the following, he tells him something quite contrary to what Mr. Nice is saying. They would like ethnically pure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's move on. Let's hear your very specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, how did you interpret what the rector of the university told you? Here it says: "Not under the Serbs and not with the Serbs." That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: To live not with somebody nor under somebody in a house does, for me, mean it's either/or.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, do you know about these stories from the time that you were there about destroyed villages that were told, and did your monitors go and check those stories out to see if they were true?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did give you one example which I'd like to refer to again, Kotlina, Gajre, and Ivaja, where these villages were said to have been destroyed. And after three days, one village had been destroyed, the other two villages had certainly been looted and to some extent devastated as well. Personally, though, I did not see villages destroyed. I did see individual houses here or there which had been destroyed but not villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you receive reports about large numbers of Albanian refugees, and did you investigate such reports if you did? Was your mission able to check reports of that kind out?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In connection yet again with the event on the three villages, Kotlina, Ivaja, and so on, I heard on the radio that approximately 4.000 refugees had arrived at the border point Djeneral Jankovic, and as it happened, one of my teams was in the area and the members of that team reported to me that up to 3 to maximum 400 people were indeed there in the general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you learn of the reasons why the population left their villages? Were you informed about that?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was linked to the fact that the population may well, at least in part, have known which of the villages or the people in the village belonged to the KLA and who might also have been using arms. In the case of these three villages, I had been told that because of the fact that there had been small fire outside directed from the villages to the Serb guard on the road from Pristina to Skopje, and that as a result of the fire directed against them, the security forces had engaged in a search. And according to the report, the people may, some of them at least, have fled the villages, but the report also made clear that the security forces moved them to, I think it was Kacanik, and the children were taken to school, the men to the police station in order to be questioned or examined there as to finding out whether there was any link between those people and the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, Mr. Hartwig, whether you had any information of any kind about the fact that the authorities or -- saying that the authorities had expelled the Albanians from their villages.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I have no knowledge of this, nor did I see any mention of it in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hartwig. And did you receive complaints that the police had been behaving improperly towards civilians? Did you receive any complaints like that?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear general -- no, I correct myself. I did not hear any complaints regarding individual police officers behaving in an improper way to civilians. Occasionally the name of the police was mentioned in connection with the arrests of Albanians which were arrested in connection with attacks or other events or people who were taken to be in remand prison. But these were all general remarks along the lines of "The police did this or that," but there were no specific complaints stating that police officers had behaved in any way severely unlawfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, was the KLA aggressive towards the Albanians as well?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes. I know from reports that Albanians were killed for the simple reason they worked either for the Serb administration or that they worked for the Serb police force. Or Albanians who were suspected of being collaborators, they were subject to a greater risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Apart from those working for the administration and the police or collaborators, can you quote any examples where a doctor might have been killed or a public personage or a humanitarian worker for not supporting the KLA, for instance?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- well, basically there was no alternative. The Albanians had to either support the KLA actively, so they had to support the KLA or even join. And I frequently heard that pressure was exerted in order to convince Albanians that it would be sensible to join the KLA. And there was a story of a doctor who I think had a birthday party near Pec, and in the course of the celebrations some men dressed in KLA uniforms entered the building and shot some of the guests in their knees or in the legs, and the -- some of the family were supposed to be forced to join the KLA as a physician. This was perhaps the most extraordinary example of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, putting it mildly, you referred to that as pressure, when people were being shot at. Mr. Hartwig, what do you know about the kidnapping of both Serbs and Albanians? So I'm not speaking only about the kidnapping of Serbs but of Albanians as well.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some time after I had received information that over 140 Serbs were alleged to have been kidnapped, talked to the president of the kidnapped Serbs in Orahovac. One of the aims of our mission was to try and effect a reconciliation and cooperation. And I asked this gentleman whether he had a list of the names of all the Serbs who had been abducted or whether he could at least give me the names of those Serbs from Orahovac who were missing. It was interesting, because he told me he could obtain that list for me but only after he had discussed it with his Albanian neighbour. My idea was that activity was in that small area of Orahovac to find out something about the whereabouts of those Serbs who had been abducted, but at the same time, I also wanted to find out where in that very same area there might be Albanian citizens who were arrested, who were kept away. I wanted to know that to relieve the minds of their relatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm expecting you conclude your examination-in-chief by the break so that we will have the other two sessions for cross-examination and your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll do my best, of course, Mr. Robinson, but this is a very important witness, and I can't omit some important questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, did the members of the KLA wear uniforms? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the KLA, I don't know whether all the members of the KLA wore uniforms, but it was customary for the great majority of people in the KLA wearing camouflage uniform, and a small part -- I mean, this sort of olive camouflage. And a small part of the people wore uniforms all in black.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were there any KLA members -- when I say were there, I don't mean exceptions, but I mean a significant number who wore civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, because obviously I can't see when I look at a civilian whether this is a member of the KLA or not. All I do know is that when, for example, the eight prisoners were released, the Yugoslav soldiers, the negotiating group of the KLA were wearing uniform at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, you haven't answered me fully. What did you know about the kidnapped Albanians? So I'm not referring to the kidnapped Serbs but to Albanians who were kidnapped by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning the whereabouts of Albanian -- Albanians abducted by the KLA, I know very little about them. Some -- some of them would have been killed. The fate of the others did not become public knowledge partly because it frequently took a long time until links could be established between a kidnapping here and a corpse found there at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any idea about the number of Albanians killed and kidnapped Albanians by the KLA? Any idea of the numbers?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I have no knowledge about this. I think that I can remember, though, that there was a time, probably mid-1999 or a little later, there was a team from Italian television, and let me repeat once again that this is not my own knowledge, this is what I have been told, and this Italian TV team was said to have reported that every second killed Albanian was killed by other Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, would you please take a look at the last page of tab 4, and the question I'm going to ask you is did the monitoring mission of the OSCE try to place under control your own monitoring mission? And before you answer that question, take a look at what it says here. "[In English] On 13 January, TM Mitrovica was chased by way by OSCE chief operation, General --" Drewienkiewicz, I suppose. That's the DZ. "-- from the place of 8 VJ soldiers' release. On 14 January, HRO had a discussion with the General DZ who clearly expressed that he considers EU KDOM superfluous. If it --" [Interpretation] Yes, superfluous, unnecessary. "[In English] If it could not be absorbed by OSCE, then at least EU KDOM should work for OSCE. It was made clear that EU KDOM, apart from its current name which was going to disappear in the near future, was going to perform its mission according to its mandate given by EU and not accept any restrictions of freedom of movement within its AOR. Final impression was that OSCE operation would like EU KDOM to disappear today rather than tomorrow." [Interpretation] Please, would you explain to me how it was that Walker's mission endeavoured to place under its control your own mission, and what was the motive for that, or, rather, what was the explanation given?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I didn't get any explanation at all for this, but I assume that essentially it was a wish on the part of General DZ, as he was generally called, as we have heard, in other words, this is organised militarily somebody is responsible for a particular area and anybody within area is subjected somewhere to the command of the person in charge and responsible for this area. Now, we as an observer mission for the European Union, we were -- we did not come under the auspices of OSCE, and therefore there was some disquiet about the fact that other observers were to be seen in this area, that they were active in this area, and basically this was the reason. But after the discussion with the general, there were no problems subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at tab 6 now, please. And it's indicative, because once again you speak of -- well, you say -- there's an explanation you give here that they are always dissatisfied, the penultimate paragraph. "Typical example for a part of the situation." "[In English] Typical example for a part of the situation: Kosovo Albanian workers are repairing and reconstructing the damaged school of Lodje; only workers with an ID can pass the control point. Sometimes individuals without personal documents delay the control and passing procedure; in order to help the Kosovo Albanians to receive their ID faster and easier, the Pec mayor asked them to come to his office and to provide just the names and few data. This was refused by the workers' speaker. Obviously, they like to continue to blame local authorities for harassment and disadvantaging them rather than reacting in a smart and normal way." [Interpretation] What does this show, then, Mr. Hartwig?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it certainly shows that there were Albanians or functionaries who tried to defuse the situation, and they tried to help where they had the possibility. And there were people who were certainly not interested in defusing the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I've understood you. You said that there were Albanians -- this Pec mayor was a Serb himself who asked them to provide documents, but they refused to do so, as it says in your report.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't refer just to Albanians here, but I could have said the same for the Serbs. On the Albanian side, there were some who tried to minimise the problems, and the mayor of Pec, who, incidentally, also had a good reputation in the Albanian region, he wanted to help to speed up the reconstruction of the school. And on the other hand, there was the workers' speaker, who didn't want assistance. He didn't want things to be simplified but he wanted to retain the status quo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we don't have much time, I'm going to go to tab 12 now. I hope I'll be able to get through what I want from that tab by the break. Take a look at this weekly assessment of the 11th of March, 1999. After the first paragraph, you say the following: "[In English] Only between the first of March -- only between the first of March and today we noticed the following incidents against police, MUP, and VJ." [Interpretation] That means we're talking about 11th of March, and it was between the 1st of March and the 11th, during those 11 days. "[In English] One police officer killed and four police officers injured in an attack against a police patrol near Kacanik on 1 March. "Two Serbs abducted in the Orahovac area by the end of February were released by KLA one Serb heavily wounded, one dead. High MUP presence --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We must have a question now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll ask my question when I have read all these separate points. This is a report which covers 11 days in the month of March. So it is the final month during which this mission was present there, the mission led by Mr. Hartwig.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll be here to the crack of dawn if you're to read all of that. It's in front of the witness, so he sees it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, you have several pages here listing the events, each one of them mentioning dead people, killings, and the like. Does all this relate to KLA attacks against the police and the army? Of course, with some exceptions. I shall read out: "One Albanian was abducted from the village of Perane by 10 Albanians wearing camouflage uniforms and armed with automatic rifles. [In English] The abducted Albanian is a member of the Albanian National minority and inspector of MUP at Prizren. "One woman at Pec was threatened by a masked and unknown person who reportedly was a KLA member. 'How can you sleep peacefully while our brothers in Drenica are dying every day?' After some questioning about her husband the woman was raped twice."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Milosevic. We have -- Mr. Milosevic, we have the point that these pages are accounts of KLA attacks. What's the question? Generally they are accounts of KLA attacks, one or two exceptions. What's the question of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the exceptions relate to attacks on Albanians. I said that the attacks were -- the KLA attacking the police and army with the exception of the cases where incidents where Albanians were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But are we dealing with KLA attacks here for the most part?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the documents received at that time, obviously it was a question of attacks by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And can you quote a single example whereby the army or police attacked anybody in Kosovo during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What period is that -- does that cover, Mr. Milosevic? 1 to 11 of March. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this witness -- Mr. Robinson, this report or these reports cover the period from January, but this last exhibit comes from the 1st to the 11th of March. But you have before you Mr. Hartwig's reports from January or, rather, the reports of his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. missions, and the notes he wrote down covering the entire period of several months, and his testimony covers the period from November 1998, in fact. So my questions relate to that entire period and his overall experience during it. So please bear that in mind with my request that these exhibits be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, before I conclude the examination-in-chief, I'm just going to read out the last sentence of this last exhibit of yours which relates to the period between the 1st and 11th of March, and it is this: "[In English] These examples are not a complaint but a demonstration of things are considered, evaluated and sold to the public." [Interpretation] Mr. Hartwig, generally speaking, is it characteristic of your testimony that there are great differences between the findings of your observer team, your monitors and your monitoring teams, and the reports coming out by the governments of the European Union and the media in the West?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to start off with a restriction here. I'm not quite sure what the European Union in general published here, but these differences between reality and practice, of course, were very clear, and they were noticeable, and I think that this did not just occur to us observers in the observing mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic, for closing your examination-in-chief. We'll now take the break for 20 minutes, and then we'll have the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can tabs 3, 4, 5, 6, 12 be exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. They will be exhibited, yes. We will take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you had asked for the admission of specific tabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We looked at the question over the break, and we are actually minded to admit all of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- as reports prepared by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that, Your Honour, I'd simply observe that the witness hasn't spoken to some three of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wasn't necessarily going to propose to ask any questions about them on the grounds that he hadn't referred to them. I raised at an earlier stage the concerns of the Prosecution, this was in a written filing, the concerns of material being produced without being referred to by the witness. Perhaps we can come back to it at the end of the evidence. I want to be brief with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I consider this exceptional. They are all matters prepared by the witness. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, was it your idea to give evidence? Did you volunteer yourself to the accused or were you asked to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How were you identified, do you know? By what publication or by what speech were you identified as somebody who might help the accused, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this happened in detail, but I do know that a report, which was sometime early in 1999, a report on the KLA also ended up in Belgrade, and I assume that this brought up the connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this one of the documents in your exhibit tab?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. That report was an individual report dealing with the expansion of the KLA. It was a report which I had put together as an individual report --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any confidential reports of that type. We spoke very openly and transmitted them openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When was your report prepared?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure any more. I assume it was probably about the end of January, February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where was it published?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was published. All I do know is that my ambassador in Belgrade contacted me, saying that he was aware that this report existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because you had published something outside the terms of your mission without authority from the ambassador, presumably.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not have needed authorisation or approval to publish, but I did not publish that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then how did this report get out? You're supposed to be -- your job is to observe something for a European bodied mission, and you then publish something separately on the KLA and it gets out into the public domain. Yes?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to repeat once again: I did not publish anything. We openly transmitted our reports to a variety of different recipients. I am not aware how many. I have once been told that about 180 recipients received our reports. I'm not aware in which way this report which was, I will repeat, not dealing with confidential matters, became part of the public domain, but it was never the intention to keep such reports secret. If that had been the case, we would have opted for a secure form of transmission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I asked you, through the Court last week, to go and check your computer. Did you do so?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I not only checked my laptop, I also checked my desktop computer in my office and I never found this paper anyway. Let me add immediately that I am well aware that people can delete reports from a computer, and I would never expose myself to such an accusation. I did write the report at the time stated, and all the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you find the letter to Lukic that I asked you to look for, through the Court?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found a letter to General Lukic. I found it in English and in German and I sent them. And in that letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of it with you?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have a copy with me but at my hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it not occur to you to bring the document here? Did it not occur to you that it was required for evidence?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then that must have been a misunderstanding. The way I understood you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. These tabs in your exhibit binder, were these documents printed for the purposes of giving evidence recently from your computer?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a binder at home in which I've collected reports that I deemed important, including this tab 1 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that's not entirely an answer to the question. Did -- these tabbed exhibits, did you print them out from your computer specially for this court hearing?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the weekly reports and everything that file was printed from my computer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So these are drafts. But we'll never know from you whether these are exactly what was sent by you to Sarajevo, will we, because these are just drafts?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is, yes, I don't know to what extent I may have rewritten or rephrased something. I have some reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make any efforts before coming to give evidence to obtain from the body to which you were providing these reports the actual documents you provided at the time? Did you make any effort?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. May I point out that mid last week, I only returned from a one-year mission to Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, if we look at the very last report that was being referred to, tab 12, and the very last sentence in it which the accused focused on, "These examples are not a complaint but a demonstration of how things are considered, evaluated --" which needs respelling -- and then in capital letters "and sold to the public." Can you just help me one way or another: Did this sentence ever form part of an official report that you sent through to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a draft of my weekly report dated 11 March. I don't know whether I sent it as it is in this draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, there are various things about your drafts, but help me with this: Did you type them yourself or did you dictate them?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such things I always typed myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because one of the oddities of the style, if you will forgive my saying so, is that when you quote something, as opposed to just putting it in quotation marks, you use the words "quote" and "unquote" time and again. And that's your style, is it? It's not a question of dictating it to someone else and somebody else typing the words "quote" and "unquote"?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quote, unquote, that's a sort of thing I learned for international communications, and if I have written that in my reports, COM, and it's COM or ECOM, it means end of comment. "Quote" is something which I've always done with international communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yourself, you were in an army for 30 years. Which army was that, the West German army?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Bundes. That's the armed forces of the Federal Republic of Germany, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When were you commissioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when did you leave the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And by that stage you'd risen to the rank of Unterleutnant, yes?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the material was incorrectly revealed on the transcript. It is now corrected. You spoke in the transcript of having command functions. What command functions did you ever hold or did you largely do non-command jobs?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was both in charge of a battalion and a company. I have held different functions in which I had command possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's now look at the mission you were actually engaged on. Do you have the mission statement here for your mission in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us what the mission's objective was.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objectives of this mission was a continuous monitoring of political, economic, cultural, and religious developments, and within the framework of our opportunities and possibilities, we were tasked to find out how cooperation could be improved between the different parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now that's a enormously wide range of activities you've identified. Let's look at it in more detail. Your mission was one of the missions generally described as the KDOMs, the US KDOM, the Russia KDOM, and so on; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I came to Pristina there were different Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Missions. One of them was the Diplomatic Observer Mission of the European Union, EU KDOM.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But these missions were, as you rather revealed, they were observer missions, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were observer missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've described your role as being to deal with political, economic, cultural and religious developments, but basically you were there to look at things and to report back.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, I think, what I described; to observe and monitor developments in those named areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You weren't negotiators or anything of that sort, were you?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one occasion when I attempted to negotiate. This concerned the case of the abducted Serbs, where I also wanted to find out whether we could get some information about the whereabouts of disappeared Albanians, but it didn't get very far because I had to go to a conference and immediately afterwards was the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were basically there to observe. And now let's deal with figures. How many people -- the accused has repeatedly said you were the head of the observers and matters of that sort. Just tell us how many people in your mission.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't have accurate figures at my disposal now, but I think at the beginning we were something like 38, 40 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at the end?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were, well, at the end not fewer, really. Perhaps some people less. Some appointments were sort of recalled by the nations involved, but I think we were still between 20 and 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if you just look, please, at tab 2 of your exhibits, last page. This is your address of uncertain date but sometime in perhaps March. And at the last page of this you make it quite clear that, "Our current task is still to provide a picture as accurate, as clear and as quickly as possible... We were not intended to be and are not competitors to OSCE..." Few lines down: "The future of the EU Attache Group ..." is that you?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "... looks pink - the smaller the better and the more beautiful." Currently, and then we see a total of 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18 people. Is that about the right figure, under 20 for your mission covering the whole of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the evacuation, yes, that would have been correct figure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And although you've given a figure of 40, on reflection and recollection isn't it true that you were always a very small mission, probably never more than 20?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. At the time when I came to Kosovo, there was a larger number of us. However, over time some observers were recalled by the individual nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In contrast, the KVM had some 2.000 people, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, look at your recording procedures. You've come to court today with none of your original notes.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: None of the actually filed reports, only drafts taken from your computer.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: None of the incoming reports from the five or so stations in which your 20 to 40 personnel were staffed?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may be able to show you one of them in due course if I'm -- if I can get it freed. I'll do my best. But not yet. You made no complaint about the reporting effectively of those 2.000 monitors working for KVM. Can you give any reason why they should, all 2.000 of them, or most of them or any of them, act in an unprofessional and improper way in the way they recorded events?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said anything like that, and I'm not aware of any unprofessionality in their reports either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You seem to be saying that the impression given by almost everybody else was false and the impression given by you was true. Are you including in those who gave a false and incorrect impression of what was happening in Kosovo the members of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. All I know is that my reports are based on the information we received and the information that existed, and our reports for a long time were also submitted to the OSCE. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just look at part of tab 4, last page of it, please. The tensions between the fully staffed OSCE of General Drewienkiewicz and yourselves revealed on the last page, and if we look at the foot of the page, we see the justification which wasn't referred to by the accused, but we look at the foot of the page, we see one of the reasons why they were concerned about your not responding, not being responsive to OSCE, because they say this: "EU KDOM should always report to OSCE when they want to operate because OSCE chiefs don't want to be responsible for the deaths of EU KDOM." If they didn't know where you were, they couldn't ensure that you were safe, could they?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a statement made by General DZ, which as far as I know he simply used as an argument, because the OSCE also had no opportunity, if we had indeed been in a crisis situation, to help us in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at a couple of examples that they reported on that you told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question is inappropriate. Mr. Nice says if they didn't know where they were, then the OSCE could not have protected their security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The OSCE mission was unarmed. Their own safety was protected by our police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with Your Honours' leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may raise that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at a couple of matters you've spoken about. I think I can deal with them in order. I hope so. But before I do, just tell me this: In order to hold the opinions you've had, and you've been very generous -- generous, you've been wide-ranging in your opinions as to where the rights and wrongs lay, have you ever taken the opportunity to review, or even to attempt to review the records by the OSCE in something called their blue book?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... why not? You're a senior military figure, you tell us with lots of experience. You're beside a 2.000 strong observer mission or Verification Mission that keeps rigorous records. Do you not think that it would have been appropriate for you to check on what others were saying and what others were reporting?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was not -- we -- well, that means I and -- or, rather, the OSCE operations and I myself had frequent meetings, and we discussed matters, and basically no agreement between us was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just before we pass from tab 4, we see that Drewienkiewicz's comment on your operation appeared to be that you'd never been seen to get out of your cars, and your response to that was that apparently he'd never seen a UK DOM, one of the 20 to 40 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is that, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The foot of the second page of tab 4. "Never seen EU KDOM leave their cars," and then on team's response he admitted he'd never seen a single EU KDOM in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were a very small operation whether you were seen to leave your cars or not, weren't you, Mr. Hartwig?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were a small mission, but we had a major advantage vis-a-vis the OSCE; namely that we spent a longer time in Kosovo, and we certainly had longer naturally evolved relationships with both sides. And from that point of view, the success or failure of our mission did not depend so much on the numbers with which we were engaged but the duration and evolution of ties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 321 is the blue book. You've told us about events at Ivaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher Mr. Nort would very kindly place on the overhead projector two pages from the reports of the 8th and 9th of March of 1999. The first page is 0352539. Thank you very much. And the second -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a systematic report with which the Chamber's familiar, and I'm sorry, Mr. Hartwig, I'm not going to have time to take you through it in systematic method, but if we look, this is something that was reported, top left-hand corner, on the 8th of March, and it says: "At 0905 hours, KLA reported that VJ/MUP attacked the village of Straza and shelled the village of Ivaja. At 1400 hours, Straza was reported burning." And then if we go to the following day, to page 03525246, on the 9th of March, same systematic method of reporting. This is what OSCE provided: "The VJ/MUP operation to clear the KLA from Djeneral Jankovic area continues. KVM patrols were initially blocked from proceeding to the affected villages. MUP or VJ forces then followed their pattern of surrounding the local villages and forcing the inhabitants to flee, through the use of direct and indirect fire. By mid-afternoon, houses were burning in Gajre, Ivaja, Straza, and Alil Mahala. MUP units appeared intent on destroying these villages." Do you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of the KVM report?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I have only a reason to question the report as far as those villages are concerned which I mentioned, which I visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us something about something that looked like a lunch break, think I. Are you aware that mosques in two of those villages were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the village, and I described the situation when I was there like a -- it looked almost like peaceful-like, during a lunch break, but I also mentioned that in that village I discovered only one -- one fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the date of your visit?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the same day when it was reported, or the next day, but on the 9th, on the 9th I remember one of the reports of one of my teams visiting these three villages, and the next day as well, and there were statements saying that there were -- those villages were not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Statements from whom?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Statements from whom?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: From one of my teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you got it here with you? Have you tried to get it from ECMM?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you attended to the evidence in this trial which includes evidence from two people, Isufu Loku and Hazbi Loku? Have you?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was not here. I can say what I mentioned. I referred to the reports that I received and what I saw myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
