utterances.text: Because they speak of the destruction of the mosques, houses burning, and 13 tanks in the area. Any reason that you can give why that evidence and why this material from the KVM is to be doubted?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any reason and I will avoid in any case any speculation, but I don't know why it is described in that way. I don't have any information on Straza and the second village you mentioned. I referred to those. I mentioned and there I can only repeat what I mentioned already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's take another example of your evidence that the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Nice, before you do, which tab was that referred to in the witness's tabs?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ivaja is referred to -- I'm sorry, I haven't got that to hand immediately, but we'll almost certainly come to it. I think it's -- yes. It may be, if Ms. Mueller helps me, it may be that he just raised it. We'll check the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now go to the tab that you were taken to by the accused this morning --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no interpretation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying I would like to assist you with regard to this question by Judge Bonomy. In tab number 12, there is the weekly assessment for the 1st to the 11th of March, and that covers the events mentioned by Mr. Nice on the 8th and 9th of March. And on page 2 already, you see that the events are described in Kotlina, Ivaja, Gajre, of the 8th and 9th of March, and the witness has already spoken of some of them, saying what he had seen. That is just one reference. And the witness has mentioned on several occasions his personal experience from these villages, what he heard and what he saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you go to tab 3, which is one of the passages you were looking at this morning, the 6th to the 13th of January, 1999. We see a very a very spare reference that the accused was seeking in his questions to amplify but you weren't able to help very much with, at the end of the first paragraph which says: "The killing of 3 MUP in a KLA ambush." If Ms. Dicklich would be good enough to lay on the overhead projector or arrange to be laid on the overhead projector from the same exhibit, 3524737. This will give you, Mr. Hartwig, some idea of the systematic method of recording because this is in daily reporting chart form. We see here at the bottom left-hand side of the chart, pointing to the general area number 2, it says: "R C1 reported that at approximately 1040 hours the KLA ambushed a MUP convoy, 4 kilometres north-east of Suva Reka. It is reported at that there are 3 MUP KIA, 3 MUP WIA --" which I suspect is killed or wounded -- "and 3 Albanian civilians were wounded." We then turn on, in the same document, to item number 2 - Mr. Nort, coming your way - we see a detailed account of what the KVM found. "Number 2. R C1 reported that prior to 1040 hours a MUP patrol consisting of 1 Lada Niva and 2 Pinzgauers was ambushed 4 kilometres north of Suva Reka," map reference given. "The patrol was fired on from well constructed, well camouflaged trenches which appeared to have been occupied for several days. The following casualties were reported." And then again, 3 KIA, 3 WIA and 3 Albanian civilians wounded who happened to drive into the ambush accidentally. "The KLA departed the area immediately following the ambush. An examination of the trenches revealed some shell or shell casings. RPG rounds were fired. The MUP apparently died whilst still inside the Pinzgauers." Any reason to doubt the accuracy of this as a detailed report of what we see in your report as the killing of three MUP in a KLA ambush?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear this is a weekly report which summarises individual events. It doesn't require detailed description because for this purpose we had daily reports that we sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have no recollection and you produce no detailed report to amplify what's in your weekly summary report, and you've made no effort to get better material from the authorities if they still hold it. Do you have any reason to doubt, please, Mr. Hartwig, the accuracy of this entry by KVM?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not doubt the report, but I am not quite clear as to the time at which we delivered our reports to OSCE as a basis for their reports. But I wanted to say something else, and that is that we wrote very detailed comprehensive reports from Sarajevo, and these certainly went on to Brussels, and what I have in my summary, in my broad outline for this period does not include these details but is intended to set up a framework - at least this was my intention - for a weekly overview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying, help me, that your reports which no longer exist or haven't been brought here match those of the KVM or are you accepting that your reports from your 20 to 40 staff were substantially less detailed than what KVM were able to provide?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Apart from what I've just read or seen, I'm not sure what OSCE otherwise transmitted or reported. We didn't get these reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... daily reporting is of exactly -- is of at least the level of detail that you've seen on these reports. Your reports better, worse, or about the same? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] It is different, and I may repeat: The daily report includes details, and my weekly report does not include the details, but it takes the events, sets that in a particular framework, and should serve as a basis for an overall assessment covering that particular week. So far it has to be different, otherwise it would become a repetition of -- of daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been able to give opinions on all sorts of matters about these events, but you only arrived there in the autumn of 1998, having no experience of Kosovo before the autumn of 1998, correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no sound experience -- yeah, experience of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you read reports from Helsinki Watch of October '89, of March 1990, of March 1993, or December of 1996, all of which were exhibits in this case, to acquaint yourself with the recorded human rights violations in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read those reports. I read other reports, one very excellent report from a British source on the -- on the situation in Kosovo, title I don't remember, and I had good luck to have somebody who was there in Kosovo since February, I think 1998, who partially experienced the development and what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on, so that we can understand what your position is, do you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of a series of reports on human rights violations prepared in the 19 -- well, late 1980s and throughout 1990s? Do you have any reason -- you said everybody got it wrong apart from you. Do you have any reason to doubt what would generally be written in Human Rights Watch reports?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only doubt what I know, and I don't know these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, in 1998 there were two Human Rights Watch reports. Did you read the one of the 1st of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's read -- have a look at what was said about one of the events you've spoken of in the report of the 1st of December, 1998. Remember you told us or you told the Judges and all of us about a mass grave? And you told us about how you went there and somebody said it wasn't a result of a killing, it was a result of a tribal fight? Remember that?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at how this has been reported in an exhibit in this case, Exhibit 198.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Mr. Nort could just lay this on the overhead projector, please. It's first of all page -- the foot of page 1. This is the document headed A Week of Terror in Drenica. Foot of page 1, please. I think -- can I have it back? I've got to find it. It's under the summary. Sorry about this. Save time if I do it this way. I hadn't checked, my mistake. The actual document being produced which is in a slightly different format than mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, this -- this is an incident, Mr. Hartwig. I'd like you follow it, please. The foot of the page begins: "The worst incident documented in this report took place in late September 1998 at the Delijaj family compound in Gornji Obrinje, a village where there had been intense fighting between government forces and the KLA that left at least --" next page, please -- "fourteen policemen dead. Special police forces retaliated by killing twenty-one members of the Delijaj family, all of them civilians, on the afternoon of Saturday, September 26. Fourteen people were killed in a nearby forest where they were hiding from government shelling, six of them women between the ages of twenty-five and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sixty-two. Five of the victims were children between eighteen months and nine years of age. Of the three men killed in the forest, two were over sixty years old. "Human Rights Watch visited the scene on September 29 while the bodies were being carried out of the forest for burial. All fourteen victims were wearing civilian clothing; most appeared to have been shot in the head at close range, and several of the bodies had been mutilated." Next paragraph: "In addition to the fourteen cases -- fourteen persons killed in the forest, seven other members of the Delijaj family were killed by government forces in and around the family compound." Does that appear to you to be the same incident that you were describing when you told us how somebody said that it wasn't forces that did the killing, it was a feudal fight?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't question that. I mentioned that it was not my observation, that I was told, and I had something like this statement that others were involved as well, like tribes or clans, more than once. So I don't believe everything which has been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think everything which encourage or which motivates one to think about things, to reinvestigate, could that really be true? To me, at least, it is always useful to get away from a firm root.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stick with my question, please, if you wouldn't mind. First of all, any reason to doubt that this is describing the incident you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is the same, I don't know. If they write it, I take it for the moment. I have no reason to doubt it or to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is there any reason, Mr. Hartwig -- you see, you've been given great licence to give opinions on everything and no challenge to your evidence. You have come along and simply said somebody said it was a tribal fight. Is there any reason to prefer, that you can identify, somebody telling you it was a tribal fight to this evidence or this material produced by experienced human rights observers, in this case Frederick Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, if it is written and -- it's accepted and a witness and whatever, I have no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Usher, could I have the book back, please. I'll find another page, and it's probably better if I do it. You see -- thank you very much. It's page 18 at the top. The page numbers are now on the top. Thanks very much

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, just to explain through to you so that you can think about this, this report, page 18, says the following: "After taking Likovac, the government forces moved on to Obrinje. According to Sejnije Delijaj, who was in Gornje Obrinje with her family at the beginning of the offensive, government forces began shelling the Delijaj compound from the direction of Likovac at around 8 a.m. on Friday, September 26, with various types of artillery and mortars. Most of the inhabitants of the compound fled to the forest to escape the shelling." Then if we turn over to page 19, please, two-thirds of the way down. Further down. Thank you very much. "According to the Pristina media centre, a media centre with close ties to the Serbian government, at least seven policemen died in the Obrinje area on September 25, 1998, the day prior to the massacre of the Delijaj family and the summary executions at nearby Golubovac." And if we can turn over to page 20, please, Mr. Nort. Foot of the page. Further down. Other way. Thanks. "On September 26, Human Rights Watch researchers observed a Yugoslav army Red Cross helicopter fly over the village of Plocica in the direction of Gornje Obrinje, which could be seen burning in the distance, and return approximately twenty minutes later." And then finally 21, please, middle of the page. A bit further up. "The village of Gornje Obrinje was largely destroyed during the Yugoslav offensive. The village was still shouldering when Human Rights Watch researchers arrived around 11 a.m. on September 29 ..." and then it goes on to deal with the shooting of cattle. Your evidence has no detail of any kind, does it, to put against a properly sourced and rooted account like this?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no eyewitnesses, that's true. There was no eyewitness, and otherwise, I repeat, I left with this or I relied on the reports we received and on the information we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, do you accept, Mr. Hartwig, that the KVM with its 2.000 observers operated a disciplined code for contacting the press and making public statements? It did it in an organised way with spokesmen at the top and other people keeping quiet. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid it would be of my disadvantage if I comment on this one. I don't blame anybody because I have no direct reason to -- to accuse or to -- to blame any -- anybody. So far -- and in addition, I don't know their daily reports. I have no reason either to question their reports. But I remember that very few hours after the dead bodies of Racak, for instance, were found, a clear statement to the media was given on who the perpetrators were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question's specific but about systems. Do you accept that the KVM was controlled and disciplined in contact with the press? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm because I wasn't a witness of any of their press conferences whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, on the other hand, after your two and a half months or nearly three months with your mission of somewhere between 20 and 40 people have felt free to comment on nearly all aspects of Kosovo history and life, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't provided comments on every aspect of life, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has given an appropriate answer to that question, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at what Klaus Naumann said. Before we look at what Klaus Naumann said - he's the senior German military man, top military officer - do you have any reason to doubt his reliability as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I don't question anything, because I don't know what you have in mind right now and what he mentioned, and in particular, I don't know what additional information apart from our information he may have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm giving you a chance before we look at the way he put things in evidence before this Court on one particular topic, I'm giving you a chance. Is there anything you know -- you're free to say this however embarrassing. Anything you know to doubt Klaus Naumann? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- how should I call it? I -- I accept the same right to General Naumann as I accept to everybody, to come to own conclusions and to have his own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I mean, somebody like the top -- you can use this, please -- the top military officer in Germany would have, apart from good lines of reporting, he would also have access to sources of intelligence it's reasonably to be inferred, correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly assume that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you just look -- I'm afraid I can't see it very clearly at the moment and I handed my only copy. A bit further down, please. Further -- that's fine. This is the way General Naumann expressed his opinion of what happened between the October agreements and the time when the bombing started, and he said this. Please listen. "It did not last for too long a time. We saw -- as of November, we saw again and again reports of violations. "I should really say, in all fairness, to the best information I got from the reports on the ground, from KDOM and later on from the Kosovo verification regime, many of the incidents were triggered by the UCK, who obviously tried to exploit the vacuum created by the withdrawn Serb security forces and who then sneaked in to take control of regions or areas. They also, I think, launched provocations, and they were not free of violence in doing that." Now, he's had access to some of your reporting but a lot of other reporting. Does his summary seem to be about right?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I understand it correctly, he admits that there were violations, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're speaking in another language. Why do you say "admit"? He simply states that there were violations. He's not taking sides. He's not defending anybody. He simply states there were violations.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well -- [Interpretation] In this case, the witness will continue in German. Now, if he states this, then certainly he will have his reason for this, and I would like to return to this. Perhaps it's a question of the point of view in observation and perhaps there is a big difference in that perhaps there are also different means of observing things from a distance or from the close proximity. I'm not saying that General Naumann is wrong or that he had assessed things incorrectly, but simply because of the proximity there can be slightly different assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the passage we looked at already casts quite a lot of responsibility on the KLA. Let's just look at the end of this short passage. Foot of the page. "The problem is that in many cases, as far as I have seen later on, particularly in the course of November and December, that the Serb side --" over the page, please -- "reacted again in a disproportionate way. It was, if I may say so, the old attitude to react to an incident where perhaps an individual had tried to kill or had killed a police officer, that they then again went in and used heavy weapons against villages and using disproportionately force against civilians." Now, just to remind you, in summary, General Naumann, looking at all the reporting, is saying lots of examples of KLA starting things off filling the vacuum left by the October agreements resulting in some disproportionate use of force by the VJ. This is the evidence the Prosecution has called. It may well be essentially the Prosecution's case. No reason to doubt it, is there? He's got it right, your general.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I can only add to the statement of General Naumann what happened I think between Christmas and the end of 1998 when suddenly the French foreign minister, followed by the French ambassador at Belgrade, followed by even the German foreign minister since Germany had taken over the EU Presidency from 1st of January, later I think even from China foreign minister or whatever, when they not warned but when they reminded UCK increasingly to stick to the rules, to consider the basis of laws, I think this somehow fits to that former statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So yes, General Naumann got it right?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, General Naumann got it right?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at a couple of other things. First of all, the letter to Sreten Lukic. Now, as you haven't brought your version with you, the version I have, and I explained that I had a secondary version, I'll explain how it comes about, Sreten Lukic was interviewed, and when he was interviewed, he read out the letter that you'd sent him. Here we have a transcript from an interpreted version of the letter, and rather than play the transcript of Sreten Lukic speaking and the interpreter translating it, it will save time if we go through this printed version of the transcript in English. If you had brought your version with you, we could have seen the original. Have you reminded yourself of what is in the version that's in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, when I wrote him I asked him whether he was this particular general I met several times in Kosovo, and I pointed out that although his information contributed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go back to my question? Have you as a matter of fact since you were here last week read the letter or your copy of the letter that you sent to Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to read what I'm going to suggest is the transcript through translation of that letter, and I'm going to ask you first of all if you recognise it as being essentially the letter that's in your hotel and I'm going to ask you for a few comments on it. The document is on the overhead projector, it reads as follows: "Dear, sir, and, General, on the 18th of March, 1999, I had to leave Kosovo on orders. At the time, I still believed in political measures and soon returned." I'll come back and ask a question about that in a minute. "What happened after my evacuation is something that I wish had never happened, and something that I would like to forget if it were possible. I'm writing these lines as a private person, and not (any longer as a member of the observer mission). With the beginning of the NATO airstrikes, I have severed my contract in the service." Just perhaps pausing there. Does this seem to you to be a transcription of, through another language, the letter that you sent to Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apart from the first sentence, this is not my typical style, "Dear, sir, and, General," and so on. This is not my style. But I think the contents is in line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far we've just seen reference to your returning. You didn't in fact return to Kosovo, did you?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You didn't return to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That may be a mistake of translation. You are described as a member, not as a leader of the observer mission. We haven't been able to find any documents dealing with you or anybody who actually knew you at the time. Were you in fact the leader of the mission or were you, as you described in evidence, a manager of the office?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the head regional office, and there was no documentation like a letter of employment or whatever. This was a decision taken by the mission headquarters, and that was the administrative decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were appointed as a member and you became, in the short period of time, the person running the office. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to the Kosovo with the information that I was going to become the head of the regional office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll read on: "I also apologise for writing in German. My Serbian is not that good. I didn't even get the opportunity to say good-bye to you and to thank you for your help and your patience with which you made clearer your view of the state of affairs and the problem of your work. Something that influenced me to a large degree, and gave me an incentive to understand you and the Yugoslav situation." So you're accepting here that you were strongly influenced by the opinions and descriptions of events given to you by Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Kosovo I followed the picture that everything which was going wrong which was crimes committed were committed by Serbs. This was my original belief more or less when I came. It was not that strong as before, but there was still something left from all that saying what the Serbs were doing and how other -- other people were suffering from. So far, he did not occupy my opinion. He did not decisively influence my today's attitude or my attitude in general, but he was a starting point to consider things in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: According to the translated version, "influenced to large degree" is the way you expressed yourself. Now, just thinking back, here is a conflict with two sides to it and different opinions being expressed publicly, and you were there for under three months. Is it safe, do you think, to find yourself strongly influenced by the chief of police of one side of a conflict like this?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one has also to consider the point of time when I wrote that letter, and that what I mentioned when I began to reconsider my own personal attitude. So far it might be misleading if you want to take the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. opportunity to use it as a starting point that I -- I was strongly influenced. It changed my mind to come to -- to a wrong decision or to a very partial attitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's read on. "The task that you had been given, until the time of your evacuation, at the end --" of our evacuation - I beg your pardon - "at the end could not be carried out, because you couldn't and weren't able to use your own means the way you thought it necessary, and which would have been most appropriate to the situation." So what was he hoping to do that he wasn't allowed to do?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That what I -- what I expressed earlier. I felt a very strong -- a very strong resistance to take action in order not to create any -- any conflict with -- with the details of the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well -- and I hope the Chamber will forgive me if I break off from the letter at this stage to return to a point that His Honour Judge Kwon launched and I wanted to develop. Do you remember you answered a question I think was started by His Honour Judge Kwon, where you said that there were common law rules favouring certain conduct of events? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, what common law rule is it that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UCK always considered itself an army, which means that they were following as [Interpretation] international law as it prevails in wartime conditions. So the KLA always considered itself to be an army, and as an army it claimed the right to abide by the rules governing international law at the time of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you gave your answer about the common law rule in relation to tab 5, which we'll look at --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small correction that has to do with the translation. "The UCK or KLA considered itself to be an army." [In English] "Always considered itself an army," that's what it says in the transcript, whereas in the Serbian interpretation is that the KLA was considered an army, which means that it was treated as an army. So it's a difference between whether somebody considers themselves to be something or whether they are treated as something, and I hope you understand the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we note the point, Mr. Milosevic. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go to tab 5, please, of your exhibits, which is the report for the 28th of January, 1999. You were asked about the last paragraph on the page, which if there's a spare copy we'll lay it on the overhead projector, otherwise, we'll just read out. You said this: "This is the classic and normal development: Attempts and assassinations by KLA against police and then ultimately search for and identify them. After the operations, weapons are hidden and the fighters convert to normal citizens with no visible link to the KLA. Since it is not the speciality of Serb forces and impossible under these conditions to surgically conduct operations, the hammering seems to remain the only response. And it can be expected that, as long as KLA applies its guerrilla tactics, the proceeding of police and MUP and VJ against KLA will remain unchanged." Hammering what, the whole vicinity, including civilians? Is that what you meant there?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- that does not mean we're talking about sort of leveling and making everything the same. Perhaps I used not a very fortunate expression here. Basically what I meant to convey was a massive use of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, a massive use of forces in reaction to small incidents is inevitably going to involve civilians being killed, and we've heard what General Naumann said about the use of the VJ. Now, were you, first of all in this report of yours, really approving of the use of hammering of areas to try and dispose of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I never approved anything. I never supported anything. My directive was and my own way was to provide information and as far as possible to leave any further conclusions to the people who read it or who receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's come become to tab 2, please, which is not numbered pages but it is the -- starting with the title page, it's the first, second, third, fourth page into tab 2, and at the top of the page it says, "... with the material status..." Do you have that page? If we come down to the last paragraph, which begins "KLA stands for Kosovo Liberation Army..." and go six lines down, you said this. This is your notes for a talk, I believe. You said: "Actions against guerrilla fighters are the most difficult military operations and, therefore, something like an area covering action seems to be the only means. This is the only method behind..." and then you go on to deal with what you say was sympathy by the international community when TV pictures are shown, and then you say this: "Finally, the liberation by the KLA and potential search or retaliation by Serb security forces turn out to be a vicious circle to the villagers; their alternative might be to either be killed by the KLA - or by Serb Security forces." Now, again, in your use of the phrase "something like area covering action," were you not reflect -- reflecting and acknowledging response of an extensive and it may be disproportionate kind where something like the KLA was involved?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may repeat, I do not support, I do not acknowledge anything of this. I just considered this from a military point -- point of view that it is most -- most difficult, and if I may remind, this was -- was a draft, but in the sense as far as those lines you were just -- or we were just talking, there is no change. I don't acknowledge anything. I don't think that any type of armed conflict is good at all. But in such a situation, decisions need to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, finally, since tab 7 is in, let's just look at tab 7 before we return to your letter to Sreten Lukic as we explore your attitude which informs this reporting. On the 4th of February, 1999, tab 7 but the last page of it, and at the top of the page where you deal with the deaths of Albanians at Rugova is something I may or may not have time to deal with, you said this: "Civilians will always be involved, concerned and hit by bullets as long as guerrilla tactics is applied and the 'freedom-fighters' hide themselves behind normal civilians ..." Were you not, in your letter to Sreten Lukic -- and let's go back to that, please, if we can lay it on the overhead projector while we're dealing with it -- were you not when you said to him because you couldn't and weren't able to use your own means the way you thought it necessary and which would have been appropriate to the situation, frankly accepting that in this type of position and in your judgement widespread retaliation with suffering for civilians was an inevitability?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, you spoke of my attitude a moment ago, and in connection with what you said just now, let me contradict that most emphatically. That is not my attitude. I am not in favour of violence in any way whatsoever and certainly never for any unlawful violence. It is simply a case, and all the last wars have confirmed this, that increasingly we see civilians being the main sufferers of war when in the past, from history, the military personnel suffered more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's read on the letter. "I have never envied you on this task and the situation, because everywhere in the world politics can impose such a task only on the army and the police. I have no insight into what happened --" pausing there for minute. You felt free to comment widely on this and that. Were you aware of efforts to internationalise the Kosovo problem in 1997, 1998 to which this accused was resistant?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. I know that there were -- that there were attempts, but as results.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know of the man Stanisic and what happened to him when he resisted the approach of the accused? Very well. Let's move on. "I have no insight into what happened after my evacuation." That holds true, does it? You have no knowledge, no insight into what happened after your departure on the 18th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't because I didn't receive any of the regular reports any more. My teams were emigrated, and whatever I was aware of, this came on -- this was a private -- private information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And although there's a -- may be a translation error at the top, you in fact did not return after the 18th of March?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not return.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You then go on to say that during your stay you sent "superiors descriptions of the situation which describe -- coincided with the real events and our assessments. Unfortunately, these efforts, as well as efforts of other observers did not yield the most wished results. Upon my return to Germany, I tried to inform the media and politicians of what I'd experienced and for what reasons truly happened. Alongside this, I drew attention to the problems which stem from the fact that the remember rebel army was politically, financially, and materially supports ambush fights against the legal executive authorities. "Here, as an individual, I have no -- have not had success, because the only things that were believed in were the things that people wanted to believe in, or what they had to believe in for political reasons. "Now, everything is viewed somewhat differently, and you will see, and it remains to be seen whether this will essentially change something in the situation. "I wish you best of luck and all the best."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask the following by way of exhibits: That this document stand as an exhibit for the time being, the witness acknowledging that it appears to be a transcription. But if before he leaves the town he could provide the versions he has in his hotel room to an associate of the accused, then a better version could be substituted for this, or alternatively, they could stand together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What arises from what you just read? It's the exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- point or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- I'm just saying that if we could put this document in as an exhibit now and get the better version later, I'd be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We haven't received a copy of it, Judge Kwon observes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you haven't received a copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry. The usher has them and hasn't provided them. I think copies are available for the -- I'm very sorry that you didn't have that, and my fault for not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have been able to free -- to locate and to free from restriction two reports of yours. Perhaps we can just look at them very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, maybe it's better to wait until the beginning of the next session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I shan't be very long, so indeed the -- unless the accused has extensive re-examination, it might be prudent for him to have his next witness available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, you heard that. You should have your next witness available. We're now going to take a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first of two, possibly three documents that I can put to the witness is a report dated the 26th of February. If the usher would be so good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you're looking at is a report dated the 26th of February from Belgrade to Pristina, subject weekly assessment Belgrade for the 26th of February. And if we look further down the page, and if the usher could lay a copy on the overhead projector, first page, it goes from Belgrade to headquarters ECMM with information copies to the various posts, one of which is Pristina regional office, the office that you were at; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document, therefore, is the compilation from Belgrade of the various inputs coming from offices such as your own; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read this report right now. I don't know whether it is a compilation and summary of my own reports or whether this is an individual report made by my Belgrade office. The office tended to use its own knowledge on the basis of our input and input coming from Montenegro and then compiling a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's turn to the second page, please, because this is reporting on Kosovo: "Although Kosovo remained relatively quiet --" which is the way the paragraph begins -- "during the period of the Rambouillet conference, there are disquieting signs that the conflict could erupt again there soon. The KLA had declared they will not give up arms." Next sentence: "Some estimates put their current strength as high as 30-40.000. Evidence of better organisation and training." Next sentence: "Nevertheless, essentially lightly armed guerrilla force." Looking at those sentences, Mr. Hartwig, does this appear to be a report that may have included contribution by yourself?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear? Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps the interpreter could repeat the answer of the witness if she's in a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The answer was that during the negotiations of Rambouillet there were periods in Kosovo which were anything but quiet...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Hartwig.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: And to that extent the opinion described here as relatively quiet I would consider to be highly subjective.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To read on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Nice, the beginning of the witness's answer was that he believed that this did not contain material from a report of his, and I don't think that's reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful to Your Honour. We'll take that as indeed part of his answer because it's consistent with the answer he's given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we read on: "Nevertheless, the KLA remains essentially a lightly armed guerrilla force. Without assistance it is no conventional map for the MUP VJ which can deploy a significant weight of artillery and armour. Already there are reports of KLA beginning to deny minor routes and specific areas to the MUP. This has not yet reached the pitch of early summer 1998 when the whole of central Kosovo was described as a liberated area. Nevertheless, the MUP will insist on their right to patrol the main routes to keep open the lines of communication between the towns where the bulk of the Serb population live." Does that appear to be a reflection of your reporting? It's quite detailed, isn't it? Who else could your organisation have to turn to but yourself?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that this is based on my reports, but at any rate, the head of the office in Belgrade was somebody I have had repeated telephone conversations with. We also paid visit to each other, and basically, yes, that was our idea of events, too. Particularly as far as the main roads and the sort of connections are concerned between the larger towns of Kosovo and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I want to reach this sentence. "Serb response to KLA activity will inevitably be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. disproportionate. They know no other way. Indeed, with an army made up largely of conscripts whose training doesn't embrace the standards required of counter-insurgency warfare, there probably is no other way." Now, we saw your earlier references to area, to hammering, to what you wrote to Sreten Lukic, the chief of police. This comment here about the inevitability of disproportionate response, that's your opinion, is it?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very obviously not my opinion. It's also the opinion of whoever wrote this report. They are basic military -- this is basic military information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the previous bit -- the previous sentence looked like being yours. Let's look at the next sentence. "The current situation then has the potential to escalate with obvious military and humanitarian consequences. It is possible that the KLA have more confidence in their armed prowess than international observers give them credit for, or it could be they do not believe that the Serbs have the stomach or the pocket for a war of attrition. Alternatively, they could be setting store by the fact that the Contact Group has noted the build-up of approximately 4.500 Serb forces ..." Where does this come from, this detail of on-the-ground position? From you?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This report was not written by me. It was written by a British colleague in Belgrade who was in charge of the office in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His name?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jocelyn [phoen]. That was the surname, Jocelyn, and the first name --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you remember it, let us know. In any event, this is a report being prepared by your office in the period February 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was not put together by my office but by the Belgrade office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I meant that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, may this become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 833.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can we turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did we have a number for the earlier exhibit? The letter to Sreten Lukic. Yes. Well, give it a number now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 834 for the extract from suspect interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look now, please, at a different topic entirely and first focus on a report dated the 23rd of October 1998. We're going back in time. We have in mind your observations last week about freedom of the press. Does the witness have a copy? Have you got a copy in front of you? No, he hasn't got a copy. Priority for the witness, please. This is a report dated the 22nd of October, when you were already, you tell us, in training, I think. We can see that it goes from Belgrade to Pristina. So may I take it that this is a report you will have seen?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't yet seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... at the time, a report coming from Belgrade to the office that you say you were running, is that a report you must have considered at the time?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see the report at that time. I only arrived four weeks after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's the 22nd of October, the date on the report, and the witness said himself that he arrived in November. So that's one month before the witness arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has given his answer anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's see -- first of all, let's see whether -- I'll come back to whether you should or did read this document in your duties as head of the office. "The law on new information came into effect today and was promulgated in the Official Gazette and the government decree on special measures of NATO threats was abolished. However, the government has yet to inform the banned dailies when their premises will be reopened for business. Nevertheless, editors of the banned papers concluded that when their premises are reopened they will not be able to maintain their paper's editorial policy under the new law. Debate now starts among the editors of the banned papers as to whether they are prepared to publish their newspapers under such conditions and at a time when the government will be keen to test the efficiency of the new law. The situation therefore remains in a state of flux for the time being. "Reaction elsewhere has been predictably hostile to the new law. The editors-in-chief of the independent Belgrade daily papers and magazines yesterday met and characterised the new Serbian law on information as an act which limits immediate media freedom." And I think that's probably all I need read on that. There were protests in Belgrade. Were you aware, taking over this office in the way that you described you did a few weeks later, of the position of suppression of a free press as described here?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, as far as I remember, I did not mention press freedom. I, rather, mentioned that the media had taken a one-sided view. I was aware that among the editors and the publishers there had been trouble. That's in the former Yugoslavia. But in my time in the Kosovo, I only once was aware of something like that when it was -- I can't remember whether it was the publisher or the editor. The magazine was Koha Ditore, and whoever it was told me if I report something which is wrong, I can be made to suffer financially in such a way I would be unable to continue my newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if we can now look at the position in Kosovo itself, and I can find -- if I can, I'll find your answers in evidence in chief about the press, but we can look, please, at the document "As Seen, As Told" at -- which is Exhibit 106 - thank you very much - and at page 309 of it. While that's coming to the overhead projector, have you, Mr. Hartwig, taken the opportunity to read either of the OSCE volumes "As Seen, As Told" or to consider them?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware that indeed there are two volumes, one focusing specifically on Serb suffering?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at what is said of the Albanian position on page 309 at the top left-hand side. "Closure of Kosovo Albanian newspapers," and I want you to comment on whether what is reported is correct, to your knowledge. "A further suppression of Kosovo Albanians' rights occurred in the form of closing down of leading Kosovo Albanian newspapers, which began on the 13th of March." When you were still there. "The Minister of Information launched the process, and the municipal court for misdemeanors issued the closure orders. "The daily Kosovo Sot and the bi-weekly Gazeta Shqiptare were prosecuted for violating the law on information by "fomenting religious and ethnic hatred after publishing a UCK picture and an article on UCK respectively." Three sentences further: "A third newspaper, the weekly Rilindja, was also reportedly prosecuted for not having registered with the Ministry of Information. Although the scheduled confiscation of equipment on the 17th of March did not happen, however, papers stopped publishing." And if Mr. Nort could take us to page 314, which is immediately after your departure but I'll ask you about it in any event. "On the 24th of March, the widely published daily newspaper Koha Ditore was charged with offences of fomenting religious and ethnic hatred similar to those levelled at the above-mentioned Kosovo Albanian papers and was fined a stiff penalty. One refugee, a lawyer and human rights activists saw Serbian forces attack the office and kill a guard." Now, this is a picture of what happened at the press just before and just after your departure. Any reason to doubt any of it?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt anything. I am aware that shortly before my departure for Sarajevo I became aware of the fact that one or two Albanian papers had been threatened with penalties or even closure. What indeed happened afterwards I do not know because it was on the 14th or 15th March in the evening that I went by car to Belgrade to Sarajevo to attend a conference there, and it was on the evening of the 17th that I returned when part of the mission had already been evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did your friend and contact Sreten Lukic justify what was happening to the press? If so, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, General Lukic is not my friend. He was one of my contacts. Second, we -- at the time that we had our discussion, we talked less about problems with the media but concentrated on current problems which he encountered within the framework of his job of maintaining security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say you talked less about the media. Yes or no: Did you discuss control of the media with him?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you think it appropriate, given your clear leanings towards and sympathies for, if I may suggest this, the Serbs, did you think it to discuss with him coming from a Western democracy, the prudence of dealing with the press in a restrictive way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let him first answer the presumption in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: His clear leanings towards and sympathies towards the Serbs. The Prosecutor is putting it to you that you have a clear leaning towards and sympathy for the Serbs. I'd like you to answer that since that's the basis for the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour [Interpretation] This is a question that I had been afraid of for some time. I have no special preference for the Serbs or anybody else. On the basis of my own personal biography, I feel obliged to try and find a way that I feel is under the given circumstances and conditions within the realms of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice, you may ask the question that follows now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you not think it prudent -- no. Did you not think it reasonable to discuss with Lukic the prudence of dealing with the press in a restricted way, restrictive way?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At those times when I had discussions with General Lukic, I discussed topical issues with him. Our meetings were not several times a week either. And had I known anything and had I wished to discuss anything along the lines you suggest with him, I would have been perfectly capable of doing so, but those newspapers which I was aware are published by the Albanians in the Kosovo were available, so I have no reason to assume that any pressure was exerted or any repressions were made vis-a-vis these publishers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few last questions about your exhibits. Tab 1. The cui bono document which you say was you discussing things with a ghost or a shadow. Shadow, I think. Now, you've gone back to your computer. Did you find this document on your computer?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not find this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So where did this document, this particular version that's been photocopied for our benefit, where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that I have a binder in which I keep documents, Xerox or my own reports. This particular report, after rereading it, I am certain I did not intend to become public knowledge, because as far as this point is concerned, I have a very clear and unequivocal statement of various issues, so I don't know who I could have sent this to. This was a personal collection of material which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If so, if you were writing in answer to a notional interlocutor, why on earth do it in English rather than German, the natural language for the best expression?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already mentioned that. Occasionally I write something in English depending -- sometimes I do that to keep in practice and sometimes because I may be more aware of background in the English language. And quite apart from that, there are some matters which occasionally, as I think you will have noticed, too, when I continued talking in English instead of going on in German.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that your answer in relation to the last page and the last paragraph of this particular report or whatever it is, where you say, "Your connection between the political development of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Kosovo is valid and correct," simply doesn't make sense unless this is a document in genuine reply to someone else. Now, thinking back, Mr. Hartwig, was this document a reply or a response to somebody with whom you were in discussion and, if so, who?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Since last Wednesday, I really spent a lot of time thinking about what could have been the origin here. I know that at some stage I simply took some facts, things I knew, sometimes very detailed, and that I think makes clear there was a dense lot of information I had available at the time, and sometimes I simply wrote this down. I have no reason why I wrote it down this way or another. Actually, I think it was irrelevant because it was a private document which was never intended to be published.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that, Mr. Nice. Mr. Hartwig, could I just ask you if you're any clearer now on the question why you have some draft reports but you don't have any of the final versions of these reports at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I wrote the drafts on my laptop computer. I made a printout of this, and after this became established, I passed it on to my office computer and then I typed in the reports again on the office computer. At that time, we didn't have any office internal link between computers and different places of work. We just had a report on which -- a computer on which the reports could be written and then sent to the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In order to save time, very quickly, please, to tab 2, second to last page, where you deal with the passing of refugees at Djeneral Jankovic crossing in the first week of March. Two questions. First of all, on the related topic of displacement of Kosovo Albanians generally, we have evidence before this court from UNHCR to the effect that by the end of March, or indeed by three-quarters of the way through March, by the 23rd of March, some 349.000-odd Kosovo Albanians were displaced, either internally or externally. Do you have any reason to doubt the figures from UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was around the 23rd of March or so, I have no reason to doubt anything here, because at that time, I was no longer in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But do you have any reason to doubt that there was generally a level of displacement of Kosovo Albanians so that by the 23rd of March, 350.000-odd were displaced?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about this because my statement related period between -- to 19th of March, and then what happened I'm afraid is beyond my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. On this page tab 2 you deal with the difference between 3.000 and 3 or 400 people at Djeneral Jankovic, but there's just this simple point: People leaving Kosovo on the first week of March were leaving because they were being forced out, whether it was 300, 400, or 3.000; correct? They were being forced out. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this because I do not know. I do not know that they were forced to leave Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You didn't speak to them?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have already said several times that as a result of a message on the radio, 3 or 4.000 refugees were said to be in this region, and a team was sent there that happened to be close by, and this team reported that there were rough -- there were roughly 300 people there and they had to be -- they had to be pushed over the frontier, they had to be forced over the frontier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've given answers to the accused about the police doing nothing wrong, the army doing nothing wrong. Here are people leaving their homes behind and, on your own observation, going to another country. You can't explain why, can you?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, and I repeat, that I referred to what we saw and heard and experienced. If people were forced out somewhere, then this is a very bad thing that I personally can quite well feel for, but I don't find it a good thing, and in this context I do not know of people having been forced out. They were people who wanted to cross the frontier. These might have been refugees, and for them it is just as bad as for others. But I do not know exactly what sort of people these were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one minute to ask you this question. We've heard a lot of evidence in this case. There's a lot of reports from human rights organisations, from OSCE about the bad things that the KLA did and about the bad things that the Serbs did. Do you not accept that people were being forced out by the VJ and/or by the MUP in the time you were there? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I did not experience it and I did not read about this in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Tab 3, please. Tab 3, last paragraph. And I'm going back to the suggestion I put to you about some favouring of the Serbs. Let's see what you said here. Foot of tab 3. This is your report, apparently, or a draft of it. It can go on the overhead projector if you've got a spare copy of it, tab 3. "The demonstrations by armed civilians - if continued - could be considered a new dimension in the conflict. Their commitment supports Serb policy, strengthens MUP and Police, is neither in contradiction to the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement, nor does it violate other political obligations. For the time being, it is not believed that the conflict will be carried into the towns of Kosovo." Now, if this is your draft report --

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and you are speaking about demonstrations by armed civilians --

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- supporting the Serb policy, yes or no, were you approving armed demonstrations by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I am not approving, but I -- I explained that amongst -- on the -- [Interpretation] that on the Serbian side an increasing mistrustfulness against everything was to be found, that according to -- that was not in order according to how one saw things then. I did not acknowledge. I did not feel this to be good. I described or -- against the -- I described against the background that these demonstrations, the armed civilians, one must also see this in conjunction with the events at the beginning of January starting off with the attacks, with the murder of the Milosevic manager, and some attacks against the police, and that on the civilian side now these measures were adopted. And therefore, naturally, the Serbian viewpoint in Kosovo was supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because time is limited. I'm going to suggest to you that the two parts of this sentences that you chose to write in English where you say their commitment supports, and you say is neither in contradiction to the Holbrooke agreement nor does it violate other political obligations is the clearest expression of approval of armed demonstrations by Serbs. But your language doesn't allow, I must suggest to you, of any other interpretation.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I have one further possibility. This -- I described this conflict situation, and I tried to state that the civil actions were not in conflict to the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement. No longer. I did not claim it to be good. Two or three times I have had to take a look at -- that this is actually a description of the facts, no more, no less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last topic, about three questions, and then final questions. Tab 4, please. We looked at tab 4, but we passed over this morning Racak. Let's look at Racak. And it's halfway down the page. We can pick it up -- well: "The fact that up to 50 or more Kosovo Albanians were killed and some of them mutilated caused and the intended or clumsy follow-on worldwide attention and an increase of the political tensions. The incident also shows the inability of authorities to properly deal with those incidents and the dissension of the people concerned." Then this: "There is, of course, justified suspect that the perpetrator(s) are amongst MUP or its active sympathisers." Now, I don't have time to go into all of this, it's available to others to read, but just tell me this: On your reporting, the MUP were those who were suspected; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that of course there was a suspicion that the dead -- that the deaths of these were due to the security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the next sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, may I just ask Mr. Hartwig. What was the basis for saying that there was justified suspect that the perpetrators are amongst the MUP? By "justified suspect," I think you mean justified suspicion. What was the basis for your saying that that suspicion was justified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were the first general statements we have heard about this issue where people said immediately this crime was committed by the security forces. I considered -- I mean, this was a brief description of what public opinion, to my knowledge, was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're just reflecting public opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not really of public opinion in the sense of what the population as a whole thought but merely the thoughts of the people I discussed this matter with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. There could hardly be more a important event for you to inquire into if you were going to do your observing properly, could there, than the Racak massacre if it was a massacre.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the letter to General Lukic confirms that I was extremely interested in this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you never found any material other than to point at the MUP.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never found anything which points at the MUP either. I only heard what observers on the spot had come up with. I heard and read what the head of the OSCE mission had made public and what we could read about this in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second question on this topic is the next paragraph, and it's to do with the judge, Mrs. Marinkovic. "The investigation of this event by Yugoslav judge became a problem as she denied to enter the place under OSCE escort. She tried to enter Racak under strong police escort, jeopardising OSCE members in place." Then at the foot of the page, or rather the beginning of the next paragraph: "Mrs. Danica Marinkovic is well known and considered a strong but clumsy on orders official." Then at the foot of the page: "So far Mrs. Marinkovic is voluntary or on order the person who significantly contributes to the increased tensions." So somewhere there was information coming to you that Judge Danica Marinkovic was not only contributing to tensions but it is reasonable to infer that she was doing so on orders. Can you tell us what that piece of information was that she was obstructive, if I can summarise it, on orders?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say she did this under orders. I simply put this with a question mark, open the possibility that theoretically this might have been ordered by people other than herself. I have no direct statement on that, and I've left this open.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let's see if I follow that. A judge does something, arguably clumsily, and you feel able, in a report disseminated widely through the former Yugoslavia through your organisation, to raise as a possibility that she's doing it on orders? Is that really what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I mean. I mean, first of all, the report was not disseminated throughout Yugoslavia; and second, I could have added a question mark, voluntarily question mark or on orders. I mean, these were the two options I saw at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, I must suggest to you that you must have had some material before you would start saying this about Judge Marinkovic. Either you can't remember or you won't tell us what the material was.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was one story which I think dealt with the issue of a mass grave, and Ms. Marinkovic intended to go there, I think for reasons of the exhumation which had to be taken place there and to do some investigative work, and we had to agree with the KLA or the UCK that this could be done without having a major escort. However, afterwards - I can't remember whether it was police or military escort involved - the whole thing then wasn't working. We couldn't do the investigation. We had to turn back. And this was the reason why I said it was clumsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two last questions on this topic and one final one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you turn over the page, Mr. Nort. You will see the third line of the -- at the top. Just look at the top, please. Next page. Thank you. Third line from the very top.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see, Mr. Hartwig - and I have a reason for asking this - that you, out of sensitivity, spell a word f... We know what the word is and we're not necessarily going to fill the airwaves with the word itself. Just tell me this: Do you recall any incident of any of your staff reporting in an inappropriate way, using language like that, to you?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The language there was not mine. It was a quote --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question is: Do you recall any incident of anybody reporting to you using inappropriate language such as that sort of language? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is a quote, then yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if I'm able at any stage to produce a document that comes from something called the mobile team of Pristina reporting to the regional office of Pristina, would that be somebody reporting to you?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of anybody reporting to you from the mobile team on events in relation to Racak or anything else in an offensive and inappropriate way?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this -- for this dreadful event, there was no reason to use swear words at all. The quote I used referred to Albanian reactions, and I simply used that in order to indicate the mood prevailing among Albanians vis-a-vis also the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, have you had a chance to think again of that last tab? I made such inquiries as I have -- been able to, the one which includes the phrase "sold to the public"? Are you sure that that report was ever sent, or was this a draft that never got sent? Tab 12.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think you asked that earlier. I have it here like this, but I don't know whether it was sent out like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Before Mr. Milosevic re-examines, I'd just like to take the witness back to the early part of the cross-examination when the Prosecutor drew his attention to the evidence of General Naumann, who testified to the disproportionate use of force by the Serbs. And the Prosecutor said, "General Naumann got it right," and your reply was, "In the right direction." I think you were speaking English at the time. I'm not certain. But could you explain to me what you mean by "in the right direction."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that -- no, not I think, but it does go in the direction --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter says this is a literal translation from the German. "It goes in the right direction" is what he means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that every state has not only the right but the obligation to oppose specific developments. The crucial point here is without doubt the way in which actions is taken and how appropriate any such action is, and when I said "in the right direction," I mean that there is an obligation on part of the state which had been exercised. However, I did not comment on the appropriateness of this action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Milosevic, we are stopping at 1.43, and I expect you to complete your re-examination by that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I hate to disappoint you, but it would be really impossible for me to finish within 15 minutes. Mr. Nice has raised a lot of issues, introducing a completely new set of documents, which I also wish to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, make a start, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hartwig, I should like to put to you a couple of questions regarding your credibility that Mr. Nice tried to assail at the beginning. Mr. Nice asked you first how come that you have come to our attention, how we identified you as a possible witness. Mr. Hartwig, was your function as head of the observers mission in Kosovo a public or a secret one?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our mission was a public one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, was it very simple, not only for me but for anyone in the Serbian and Yugoslav public to become aware of the identity of the head of mission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Having gotten the reply that -- [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I got the answer that it was public. This mystification about how we identified Mr. Hartwig is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't bother with the comments, Mr. Milosevic. Let's move on.
