utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as for your qualifications, please confirm the following set of questions with only a yes or no. You had military training until 1962. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After that, were you commander of a platoon in the German army? Sorry, until 1964.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From 1964 to 1993, did you occupy a variety of functions in the field and in headquarters such as commander of various units, staff officer, member of the headquarters, positions in higher headquarters at battalion, company level involving command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive appointments in the NATO?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From October 1995 until March 1996, were you involved in the work of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From May 1996 until January 1998, were you in the transitional administration of the United Nations for Baranja, Eastern Srem, and that area?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From July 1998 until October 1998, were you part of the observers mission of the European Union?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say it sounds like the accused is reading from and leading a curriculum vitae that hasn't been provided to us. Normally I wouldn't object, but as a matter of fact if we were provided with curriculum vitae in advance and not the limited material we've been given, we would be much better able to deal with witnesses and therefore I do object to him raising this matter in a leading way at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's not clear to me to what -- to what does this relate, what part of the cross-examination, and in any event, it is -- these are -- let me finish. These are matters that you really should have raised in your examination-in-chief at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't cross my mind, Mr. Robinson, that Mr. Nice would challenge the qualifications of this witness and his competency. What is at stake here are facts that confirm his qualifications and his competency as a witness. Mr. Nice went so far as to ask him if he had been indeed head of mission, which to my mind was impolite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The point is you can't lead in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are not leading questions. These are factual questions regarding previous posts of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there is a difference. If you had put it at the beginning of your examination-in-chief, you could have led to them because, at that time, there was no issue. There was no contention about it. But now that it has been become contentious in re-examination, you can't lead to it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm not going to ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, Mr. Nice said, and I noted it down, you had spent less than three months in Kosovo. How long did you exactly spend in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arriving 20th of November, 1998, and leaving 19th March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We need not do the maths now. Thank you for this answer. Mr. Nice asked you at one point to quote from the last paragraph of tab 3, and he asked you to confirm on this basis that you were biased. "[In English] Their commitment supports Serb policy, strengthens MUP and Police, is neither in contradiction to the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement nor does it violate other political obligations." [Interpretation] What I just read, does it have anything to do with what is written at the beginning of this same report on the same page? Please look at tab 3. You say what characterises this previous week. This is the weekly assessment. And you are saying that it affects the entire political situation, and you say: "Those events were the explosion of a hand grenade in front of a cafe in Pristina, [In English] the murder of the Serb manager of the Obilic power plant, the killing of 3 MUP in a KLA ambush, and the capturing of 8 VJ soldiers by KLA." [Interpretation] And in the next paragraph you say: "[In English]... resulted in public Serb demands for better protection." [Interpretation] So these tragic events within just a few days that you enumerated in paragraph 1, is it the case that this caused the reaction of Serb civilians and their requests to be protected?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was most certainly the catalyst for turmoil among the Serbs, and this, the fact that they were then partially armed or armed themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next tab, relating to investigative judge Marinkovic, Mr. Nice asked you which order you were talking about, and that's why I have to read this paragraph, in order to show what in fact you were saying: "... seizure of the Racak victims out of the mosque and [In English] the day the need to be buried according to religious rules and the international [sic] forensic examination without presence of OSCE KDOM --" internal -- [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreter -- "[In English] forensic examination without presence of OSCE EU KDOM, Kosovo Albanians or media representatives increased reservations and nourished the suspect that something will be manipulated. So far, Mrs. Marinkovic is - voluntarily or on order - the person which significantly -- which significantly contributes to the increased tensions." [Interpretation] Are you speaking here about the steps taken by Mrs. Marinkovic as investigative judge in order to conduct an investigation regarding the victims of Racak or something else that she's doing in circumvention of the regulations?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said a moment ago that there was a minor story where despite other agreements, police followed. And I simply quoted that story in order to make clear that what happened there happened at another place, too; namely, that the work of an investigating judge is also a job which is not recognised as being necessary everywhere but which sometimes can contribute to tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not call into question the actions taken by Mrs. Marinkovic in her capacity as investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never doubted or criticised the way the job was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hartwig. A little while ago you said that you heard about Racak, what the Verification Mission said. I suppose you meant Mr. Walker, because he spoke on behalf of the Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the OSCE, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn later, however, that what Mr. Walker stated at the time was not true?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It seems to me that may constitute a significant leading question. I'm not quite sure whether it falls within the ambit of this witness to deal with. I have 30 seconds of something to say before we close today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not clear to me, Mr. Nice. Why do you say it's -- he's asking whether he learned later that what Mr. Walker said was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that -- that contains within it a suggestion that what he said wasn't true. That contains a suggestion in it that what he said wasn't true. It's clearly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he can answer it, and then we'll have to -- we will have to adjourn because there is another case starting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later I simply read reports and newspapers that had been broadcast on the radio. The big question regarding Racak, as far as I'm concerned, is bearing in mind what I described earlier, namely that from the end of 1998, increasingly the Serbs received sort of worldwide sympathy. There were loss of expressions of sympathy from all over the world, and the UCK was requested to keep within the bounds of the law. And then the dreadful events in Racak would have been an almost expected -- or an event such as Racak was almost something which was on the cards. It could be expected to happen, that somehow something would happen to get the mood to change. I don't know what really happened but I put Racak in that particular time frame, which was a very sort of time window which is restricted where suddenly the Yugoslavs received sympathy, and that's all that I connect with the Racak incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice, quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the next witness, Mr. Lituchy, having reviewed the exhibits provided by the accused, may well argue tomorrow that the evidence is inadmissible. I mention that now so that the accused can be on notice that he may have to justify the relevance of material he seeks to produce, and it may be of assistance for the Court if the Court has an opportunity to review the served exhibits in advance, and of course it may be prudent for the accused to have his following witness available in case the evidence is taken shortly or ruled inadmissible. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic is put on notice, also the Chamber. Tomorrow we will be without a translator, but I think we can manage. Can you manage without the translator, Mr. Hartwig?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will go on the slippery ice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's hope you stay up. We will adjourn now until tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
